source.title: Overparameterization and Generalization Error: Weighted Trigonometric Interpolation
source.authors: Yuege Xie; Hung-Hsu Chou; Holger Rauhut; Rachel A. Ward

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes and measures generalization-risk curves in a weighted Fourier interpolation model, rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The study directly analyzes and measures risk as the number of Fourier features varies. Its discussion of double descent in other papers is cited background, not evidence counted here. It does not report results on risk over training epochs or a sample-size sweep showing that more data raises risk.
record.test_reason: The paper derives exact risk and measures empirical risk as Fourier feature count p sweeps past n in a linear interpolation model. That bears on V4, whether risk improves past the interpolation point outside deep nets. It is a different, analytic method aimed at the same question. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Exact non-asymptotic risk expressions show that a bias toward smooth interpolants (weighted min-norm trigonometric interpolation) lowers overparameterized risk. Under q ≥ r ≥ 1 this risk falls strictly below the best underparameterized risk. The authors present this as a contribution to understanding the double descent curve. Plain min-norm interpolation gives no such benefit.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses weighted or plain trigonometric interpolation with equispaced samples and random decaying Fourier coefficients, rather than the original deep-network size and training experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Risk behavior depends on the coefficient-decay parameter r and the estimator weight parameter q; the study reports different trends for different values of these parameters.
record.peer_reviewed: SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science
record.problems: The experiment uses a specific Fourier model and reports 100-run empirical averages; several curve values are only shown in figures. The results do not test neural networks, epochs, or a sample-size increase near the threshold.

untested.parts: No sample-size sweep; n is fixed in all risk curves.
Only one linear Fourier model class with equispaced samples; no other model classes.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
No label-noise sweep; no tuned ridge regularization; no multiple descents.

missing.what: Plain min-norm (q=0) risk after p > n. It rises suddenly to about 1 and is higher than underparameterized risks when r > 1. At p = D, risk0 = 1 − n/D.
missing.locator: Appendix C.1, Figure 6; Remark 3.2; Figure 3 text

missing.what: Shape of the underparameterized risk curve as r varies. It increases with p for r = 0, becomes U-shaped at intermediate r, and decreases monotonically for r ≥ 1.
Choice of q. Weighted estimator risk is lowest at q = r, and is robust for q near r.

record.verdict_notes: The study is mainly theoretical, with Monte Carlo checks: D=1024, n=64, 100 runs. The weighted estimator acts as an implicit regulariser, but it is not tuned ridge, so V6 is untested. The conclusion mentions, without data, that with random sampling points the risk blows up around p = n, which suggests a sharper peak. The plain min-norm estimator is the one analysed by Belkin, Hsu and Xu; here it fails to beat the underparameterized regime for smooth targets. T3 (new setting) would also be defensible as the tranche.

versions.untested_parts: Deep networks and model-wise double descent specifically in deep networks.
Risk over training epochs or training time.
Whether increasing training samples near the interpolation threshold raises test error.
The study analyzes a Fourier interpolation model, not a broad range of model classes; it does not establish the claim across model classes generally.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
Whether label noise or variance drives the peak, whether peaks split into multiple descents, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
Whether counting complexity by an effective number of parameters turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: random Fourier series model
rows.operation_detail: Compare the lowest theoretical risk in the overparameterized regime with the lowest risk in the underparameterized regime.
rows.measure: Lowest generalization risk by parameter regime
rows.baseline: Lowest possible risk in the underparameterized regime
rows.value: The lowest risk in the overparameterized regime is strictly less than the lowest possible risk in the underparameterized regime.
rows.note: This establishes a lower achievable risk beyond the interpolation threshold under stated conditions, but does not by itself establish the full curve shape.
rows.check: Theorem 4.4(b) states the core V4 claim: for q ≥ r ≥ 1, the best overparameterized risk is strictly below the best underparameterized risk. This is a theoretical result, not an empirical measurement. Part (a) also shows underparameterized risk decreasing monotonically, so there is no classical U in this regime. Observed fits better than partial.

relationships.condition: Weighted min-norm estimator biased toward smooth interpolants (q = r = 0.5 empirically; q ≥ r ≥ 1 theoretically)
relationships.reason: The authors report non-degenerate double descent at r = q = 0.5 (R1). Theorem 4.4 proves best overparameterized risk is below best underparameterized risk (R7).
relationships.display_finding: Experiments showed non-degenerate double descent at q=r=0.5, and theory for q≥r≥1 established lower optimal risk beyond interpolation than below it.

relationships.reason: From text, not rows: Appendix C says plain-estimator risk jumps to about 1 after p > n. It stays above underparameterized risk when r > 1, and Fig. 3 calls plain overparameterization 'useless'. The second descent below the first minimum therefore depends on the estimator's smoothness bias.
relationships.display_finding: Risk jumped to about 1 after p > n and remained above underparameterized risk for r > 1, making superiority to the first minimum dependent on smoothness bias.
